dossier.public_summary: The dips are not the same every orbit: odd and even eclipses differ by more than a factor of two and a second dip shows up halfway around the orbit, both with the depth expected for a star eclipsing a star, not a planet. Depths also change from one sector to the next and from transit to transit, which a planet would not do. Together this is best explained as an eclipsing binary.

reasons.why: Odd and even eclipses differ at >5 sigma with depth ratio 2.2, the classic signature of a binary folded at twice the true period (28.4 d). This is not random noise and positively favours an eclipsing binary on the target over a planet.

A significant secondary dip at phase 0.6444 with depth about one-quarter of the primary (178.1 ppm vs 767.6 ppm) is seen. A planet at this size would not show a 5.5-sigma secondary, but a stellar companion at ~half phase does.

Depth changes dramatically between sectors (p_constant=0.0001968) and between individual transits (p_consistent~4e-27) with one epoch at -6 ppm essentially flat. A true planet must have consistent depth; this scatter favours a variable/binary/blended signal and a few bad transits.

reasons.why: Independent planet scorer ranks this in the bottom 86% planet-like tail (0.14), consistent with the odd/even and secondary evidence and the flat-bottom V-shape (v_sigma -2.407) not outweighing them.
